children: September opens with an oil pump, a global bond selloff and the first clue before Friday’s jobs report.
Tech faces a volatile September
Nasdaq futures edged lower Tuesday after the Composite slipped 0.1% Monday. The S&P 500 lost 0.3%, while the Dow fell 374 points, or 0.7%.
All three still gained in August, but September has opened with considerably less enthusiasm for your favorite expensive assets.

The immediate problem is the US ten-year Treasury yield, which climbed toward 4.78%, near a 20-month high. Higher yields make bonds more competitive and reduce the present value of future corporate earnings. That calculation is particularly unfriendly toward technology companies priced for years of ambitious growth.
Markets now assign roughly a 65% probability to a September Fed rate increase following Chair Kevin Warsh’s hawkish Jackson Hole speech.
Rate-sensitive software and semiconductor stocks begin the month competing against both a more demanding central bank and bonds that suddenly offer respectable returns.
Oil pours inflation onto the fire
Brent crude crossed $91 after renewed US–Iran attacks revived fears of further disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. WTI climbed toward $87.
The waterway handled roughly one-fifth of global oil flows before its closure, making every fresh projectile an unwanted inflation indicator.

Higher energy costs threaten corporate margins and consumer spending while making it harder for inflation to return to the Fed’s 2% target. Energy shares benefited Monday, but most other sectors weakened.
What helps an oil producer can become a rather expensive problem for practically everyone using electricity, fuel or transport.

The bond selloff is global. Japanese ten-year yields approached 3% for the first time in a generation, while long-term German and French yields reached roughly 15-year highs. Japan’s Nikkei slipped as chipmakers Tokyo Electron, Renesas and Lasertec fell between 3% and 4%.
Jobs data meets enormous AI spending

July job openings arrive Tuesday at 10:00 a.m. ET, with forecasts near 7.33 million. Strong demand for workers could reinforce rate-hike expectations; a sharp decline may provide relief for yields and tech.
remains the larger test, with only about 50,000 new jobs expected.
Nvidia received a fresh demand signal after Anthropic said it signed a $35 billion cloud-computing agreement with Nvidia-backed Lambda.
The Texas project involves roughly 350 megawatts of data-center capacity. Apparently, AI’s appetite now requires contracts measured in national infrastructure budgets.
Elsewhere, Amazon remains under pressure following reports of another possible FTC case, while Shein fell after its Hong Kong debut.

Gold slipped toward $4,430 and Bitcoin hovered around $78,000. Nasdaq enthusiasts might want to watch ten-year yields, $91 Brent and JOLTS — the index’s next move may begin outside the technology sector.
